Take each square to have side length \(1\), with coordinates \((0,0)\) at the lower-left corner.

**Square I:**  
The two lines are
\[
y=1-x \quad\text{(from top-left to bottom-right)}
\]
and
\[
y=2x \quad\text{(from bottom-left to top midpoint)}.
\]
They meet when
\[
1-x=2x \Rightarrow x=\frac13,\quad y=\frac23.
\]
The shaded triangle has base \(1\) and height \(\frac23\), so
\[
S_I=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac23=\frac13.
\]

**Square II:**  
The lines are
\[
y=1-x \quad\text{and}\quad y=\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
1-x=\frac{x}{2}\Rightarrow x=\frac23,\quad y=\frac13.
\]
The shaded triangle has height \(\frac13\), so
\[
S_{II}=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac13=\frac16.
\]

**Square III:**  
The lines are
\[
y=1-2x \quad\text{and}\quad y=\frac{x}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
1-2x=\frac{x}{2}\Rightarrow x=\frac25,\quad y=\frac15.
\]
The shaded triangle has vertical base \(1\) and horizontal height \(\frac25\), so
\[
S_{III}=\frac12\cdot1\cdot\frac25=\frac15.
\]

Since
\[
\frac16<\frac15<\frac13,
\]
we have
\[
\boxed{\text{C: }S_{II}<S_{III}<S_I}.
\]

(Equivalently, \(S_I:S_{II}:S_{III}=10:5:6\), so \(S_{II}<S_{III}<S_I\).)
